summary.summary:
Scope: single log source available, ssh.log (OpenSSH server on host "co1508kali2"), 28 lines covering 2026-10-23T10:38:38Z to 10:41:45Z. No other logs (web, other auth) were present in this workspace.

Timeline of the incident:
- 10:38:38Z: sshd starts normally, begins listening on port 22 (IPv4 and IPv6). This is baseline service start, not attacker activity.
- 10:39:48Z - 10:39:50Z: A burst of 8 connections from 192.168.92.129 hits the SSH daemon within 2 seconds. None of these complete a normal SSH handshake:
  * One connection fails at "kex_exchange_identification" (client closed before banner exchange finished).
  * Two connections fail with "Protocol major versions differ: 2 vs. 1" - i.e. the client tried to speak SSHv1, which this server does not support.
  * Four connections fail with "Unable to negotiate... no matching host key type found", each offering a different host key algorithm in turn: ssh-dss, ssh-rsa, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521.
  * Remaining connections are closed immediately [preauth] (before authentication even started).
- 10:41:43Z - 10:41:45Z: The exact same pattern repeats from the same IP, 192.168.92.129 - another 8-connection burst testing SSHv1 fallback plus the same four host-key algorithms in the same order.

Interpretation: every single failure here happens during the pre-authentication key-exchange/protocol-negotiation phase. No username or password was ever submitted (auth_summary found 0 failed logins, and a direct search for Accepted/Failed/Invalid user/sudo/useradd returned zero matches). This is NOT a credential brute-force attempt - it is a classic SSH fingerprinting/enumeration scan, consistent with tools like `nmap --script ssh2-enum-algos,ssh-hostkey` or `ssh-audit`, which deliberately iterate through SSH protocol versions and host-key algorithms to map what the server supports (useful for an attacker to pick an exploit or downgrade path, or to catalog weak/legacy algorithms such as ssh-dss and SSHv1 that this server correctly rejected). The two bursts ~2 minutes apart suggest either a retried scan or two scan modules run back-to-back by the same tool/operator.

No evidence in this log of a successful login, privilege escalation, account creation, or lateral movement - the activity is confined to recon against the SSH service itself. Because only ssh.log was provided, I cannot confirm whether 192.168.92.129 was also seen hitting a web service or other hosts; that correlation could not be performed here due to lack of other log sources.

findings.title: SSH protocol/host-key algorithm enumeration scan from 192.168.92.129
findings.evidence: 2026-10-23T10:39:48+0000 co1508kali2 sshd[8421]: Unable to negotiate with 192.168.92.129 port 58868: no matching host key type found. Their offer: ssh-dss [preauth]
findings.recommendation: Treat 192.168.92.129 as a scanning source. Correlate with firewall/NetFlow and any web/other service logs for this IP (none were available in this workspace) to see if the scan expanded beyond SSH. Consider rate-limiting or blocking repeat scan sources at the perimeter, and ensure fail2ban or equivalent is enabled to throttle rapid repeated connections even when they never reach authentication.

findings.title: Legacy/weak algorithm probing (SSHv1 downgrade attempt, ssh-dss)
findings.evidence: 2026-10-23T10:39:48+0000 co1508kali2 sshd[8419]: error: Protocol major versions differ: 2 vs. 1
findings.recommendation: No action needed on the server itself since it correctly rejected SSHv1 and the ssh-dss/weak key types - this confirms the server configuration is hardened. Document this as a positive control validation, and keep monitoring for any future client that manages to negotiate a legacy algorithm successfully.

findings.title: Repeated identical scan burst (two waves ~2 minutes apart)
findings.evidence: 2026-10-23T10:41:43+0000 co1508kali2 sshd[9764]: error: kex_exchange_identification: Connection closed by remote host
findings.recommendation: The repetition suggests an automated scanning tool or script re-run rather than manual probing. Flag 192.168.92.129 for continued monitoring in case it returns with an actual authentication attempt (username/password) following this recon phase.

next_steps: Check firewall/IDS/NetFlow logs for 192.168.92.129 to see if it touched other services (HTTP, RDP, etc.) around the same time window (10:38-10:42 UTC on 2026-10-23).

If other log sources exist outside this workspace (web server, additional auth logs, EDR), pull them and re-run the timeline tool filtered on 192.168.92.129 to check for follow-on exploitation after the recon.
Add 192.168.92.129 to a watchlist; if it reappears with actual authentication attempts (Accepted/Failed password entries), escalate to a brute-force investigation (T1110).

Confirm sshd configuration explicitly disables SSHv1 and weak host-key types (ssh-dss) via sshd_config - the logs show it is currently rejecting them correctly, so capture this as a baseline/config attestation.

No credentials were compromised and no further action is required on the host itself at this time beyond monitoring; this is a low-urgency recon event unless paired with later authentication evidence.
